(a) Assessment Required.—The Secretary of Defense shall—
        (1) utilize a defense federally funded research and development center to carry out an assessment of the effectiveness of the Defense Experimental Program to Stimulate Competitive Research; and 
        (2) not later than nine months after the date of the enactment of this Act, submit to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives a report on that assessment.  
    (b) Matters Assessed.—The report under subsection (a) shall include the following:
        (1) A description and assessment of the tangible results and progress toward the objectives of the program, including—
            (A) an identification of any past program activities that led to, or were fundamental to, applications used by, or supportive of, operational users; and 
            (B) an assessment of whether the program has expanded the national research infrastructure.  
        (2) An assessment whether the activities undertaken under the program are consistent with the statute authorizing the program. 
        (3) An assessment whether the various elements of the program, such as structure, funding, staffing, project solicitation and selection, and administration, are working effectively and efficiently to support the effective execution of the program. 
        (4) A description and assessment of past and ongoing activities of State planning committees under the program in supporting the achievement of the objectives of the program. 
        (5) An analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of having an institution-based formula for qualification to participate in the program when compared with the advantages and disadvantages of having a State-based formula for qualification to participate in supporting defense missions and the objective of expanding the Nation’s defense research infrastructure. 
        (6) An identification of mechanisms for improving the management and implementation of the program, including modification of the statute authorizing the program, Department regulations, program structure, funding levels, funding strategy, or the activities of the State committees. 
        (7) Any other matters the Secretary considers appropriate.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that using a federally funded research and development center, and the mention of State planning committees, brings outside parties into the process. But the center only carries out an assessment whose results go to congressional committees, so it produces a study and report rather than giving input on a federal decision, and Congress is inside the federal government. The State committees are only a subject of the assessment; they are not consulted on anything. There is no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking or right to sue.
fable.s: utilize a defense federally funded research and development center to carry out an assessment of the effectiveness of the Defense Experimental Program to Stimulate Competitive Research

qwen_block.w: The section requires the Secretary of Defense to conduct an assessment and submit a report to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is internal government communication, not participation by outside parties. Although the assessment mentions 'State planning committees,' the text only requires the Secretary to assess their activities, not to consult with them or involve them in the decision-making process for the assessment itself.
qwen_block.s: submit to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives a report on that assessment

opus.w: This section requires a study and a report to congressional committees, and Congress is inside the federal government. Using an FFRDC to do the assessment is like hiring a contractor to produce a study. It is not consultation with outsiders before a federal decision, as Example 3 shows. The mention of State planning committees only names a topic the report must evaluate. It does not give those committees any role in a federal decision.
opus.s:

        (2) not later than nine months after the date of the enactment of this Act, submit to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives a report on that assessment.
opus.b: 1. **Tempting-but-wrong reading:** The Secretary must use a federally funded research and development center (FFRDC), a non-federal entity, to run the assessment, and the report must discuss "State planning committees." That could look like outsiders taking part. It fails because the FFRDC only carries out a study, and the report goes to the congressional Armed Services Committees, which are inside the federal government. No federal decision depends on outside input. The State committees are only things the study assesses, not parties consulted before a decision. This matches Example 3, where consulting outside experts on a study's contents was not participation.

qwen_chat.w: This section requires the Secretary of Defense to conduct an assessment using a federally funded research center and submit a report to Congress. Both the research center and Congress are inside the federal government. There is no requirement to consult with or coordinate with outside parties (such as states, tribes, or the public) before making a decision. The mention of 'State planning committees' is limited to assessing their past activities, not consulting with them.
qwen_chat.s: (a) Assessment Required.—The Secretary of Defense shall— (1) utilize a defense federally funded research and development center to carry out an assessment of the effectiveness of the Defense Experimental Program to Stimulate Competitive Research; and (2) not later than nine months after the date of the enactment of this Act, submit to the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and the House of Representatives a report on that assessment.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the assessment involves "State planning committees" and potentially external research centers, it constitutes participation. However, the section only requires the Secretary to *assess* these entities and report to Congress. It does not require the Secretary to consult with them, coordinate with them before making a decision, or include them in an advisory body. The interaction is one-way (assessment/reporting) rather than collaborative or consultative. The report is submitted to Congress (inside government), and the assessment is conducted by a federally funded center (inside government).
